title: Why and Where: A Characterization of Data Provenance
research_question: How can the provenance of query-produced data be formally characterized and computed in terms of both why an output exists and where its values originated, while remaining meaningful under query rewriting and view composition?
methodology: The paper uses a formal database-theory methodology based on a deterministic semistructured data model with explicit source locations and a query language called DQL. It defines normal forms and a rewrite system, then formalizes why-provenance through witnesses and witness bases and where-provenance through source paths and derivation bases. The authors prove normalization, soundness, completeness, invariance, and query-composition results and use worked relational and hierarchical-data examples rather than empirical experiments.

key_findings.finding: The paper distinguishes why-provenance, which identifies source data responsible for an output's existence, from where-provenance, which identifies source locations from which particular output values were obtained.
key_findings.section: Sections 1 and 4, Introduction and Two Meanings of Provenance

key_findings.finding: Every well-formed query in the defined language has an equivalent normal form reachable through a strongly normalizing rewrite system.
For a normal-form query and singular output value, the proposed Why procedure computes the same witness basis as the formal provenance definition.

Although a query-dependent witness basis is not invariant under all equivalent formulations, its minimal witness basis is invariant for equivalent well-formed queries restricted to equality conditions, with stated extensions to some inequality subclasses.
Why-provenance can be propagated through materialized views so that recursively tracing witnesses through views agrees with composing the views out of the query.

Where-provenance is not generally invariant under equivalent query rewritings, but the paper identifies a restricted class of traceable queries whose derivation basis is preserved by its rewrite system.

limitations: The analysis is restricted to well-formed and well-defined queries under the paper's DQL assumptions.

Variables are restricted to singular values, and DQL is explicitly less expressive than XML-QL in several respects, including lack of Kleene-star path patterns and limitations on nested-query and Skolem-function forms.
A general semantic characterization of where-provenance is not established; rewrite invariance is obtained only for the restricted traceable-query class.
The strongest minimal-witness invariance result is stated for equality conditions, with only some subclasses involving inequalities covered.
Some XML translation and comparison details are deferred to a fuller version.
The paper establishes formal properties but provides no empirical performance or scalability evaluation.
The framework explains derivation provenance of query results rather than temporal version histories of corrections, supersessions, or reopened records.
raw_claims: Why-provenance concerns the source data whose presence accounts for an output's existence.
Where-provenance concerns the source location or locations from which a particular output value was extracted.
The deterministic data model gives every represented node a uniquely describable path.
DQL can express positive select-project-join-union relational queries and positive nested relational algebra under the paper's restrictions.
The rewrite system reaches a normal form from every well-formed query in finitely many rewrite steps.
A witness is a source substructure sufficient for producing the output under the query.
The Why procedure is sound and complete for the witness basis of normal-form queries and singular output values.
Minimal witness bases are invariant across equivalent well-formed queries using equality conditions.
Provenance traced through materialized views agrees with provenance after the views are composed out of the query.
Where-provenance is more sensitive than why-provenance to the syntactic form of equivalent queries.
For traceable queries, derivation bases used for where-provenance are preserved by the specified rewrite system.
